decision.audit_notes: Verified current-session dialogue; decision evidence remapped to cleaned source.

evidence.text: That a good one? … I too really want to invest in this company. I think your round is all of a sudden over-subscribed. So I'm feeling a little like I've got to be scrappy here. We're a small fund. I'd like to do $50,000. But I think what you're working on is amazing. I think you're making a difference in the world, a positive difference. And I think you're going to make a boatload of money. And when I can combine those two things, it really gets me excited.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. Socks off. Alright cool. Um, so, hello everyone, my name is Juan-Pablo Segura, I'm one of the founders of Babyscripts. Growing up in a family of six, my mother being pregnant was a very familiar and beautiful concept with my siblings and I growing up. But it was also a scary time. My mother actually suffered from three miscarriages. The reasons why were beyond any person or doctor's understanding. No one knows why problems still to this day occur in pregnancy.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: And so we said, you know what? Technology and big data can start answering some of these questions.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: There is no company that has been able to really take connected medical devices and make them the standard of care. And everyone's talking about taking costs out of the hospital which is really expensive and into the home. You can't do that without connected medical devices.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: There's a blood pressure cuff and a weight scale that are both connected to the internet...

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So blood pressure is too high, too much weight gain or weight loss in a week, and if anything is wrong we tell the patient's doctor in real time so that the doctor can intervene.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So this is what to expect when you're expecting put onto an app?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Pretty much. We've essentially been able to automate a lot of prenatal care using our devices and our app. Instead of patients going in 14 times to see their doctor, through Babyscripts, patients only go in 8 times.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Do patients mind not having as many doctor's appointments? Because, I mean, there's, I know, I've been pregnant four times. The thought is, is that, you worry every time, right?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That peace of mind when you go to the doctor.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah. You actually look forward to going to the doctor, and yes.

turns.speaker: Juan
turns.text: Yeah so, we knew that that question would come up. When we talked to doctors, obviously patient satisfaction is very important. Like for example we've published two studies really showing the efficacy of the product.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I would think personally, if a doctor were to say to me, “listen, I’m going to give you this kit, now I'm not going to, I'm only going to see you half of the time, this will take care of the rest of it,” I would have a problem with that, actually.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah, so that's really where the controlled study was very important for us. And the way that we position the product. So #1, I mean we've proven that patients are more satisfied.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How many women did you study?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So it was 50 on Babyscripts, with the optimized visit schedule being remote monitored.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, it's only 50 women.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: But it actually it was powered clinically enough to be able to make a claim on it. Like, we took a very educated and scientific approach to it. So it was a powered study focused on satisfaction.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: You know, we’re generating 30 times the amount of data and touchpoints, um.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But how can you generate that much data just from a scale and a cuff? Isn't that just the weight and the blood pressure?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Well, the reason why prenatal care exists as a category is actually to manage blood pressure. Everything else is an extension. So if you look at every visit that occurs in the pregnancy experience, you're always checking weight, always checking blood pressure, and answering questions. There are some visits where you're doing more, right. Ultrasounds, genetic tests. And we're not eliminating or optimizing those appointments. We're really focused on the routine appointments that occur early in the pregnancy, and a few a little later on in the pregnancy.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But you would think that the patient — in order to have that peace of mind that they would get going to the doctor's office, where the doctor looks at them, checks the blood pressure, checks the weight, and says “you're looking good,” thumbs up — you would think that they would want that kind of reassurance each time that the doctor gets the measurements in order to have that increased peace of mind.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And listens to the baby, you listen to the baby's heart.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah sure.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I mean, there's a lot of things. You know, I'm a little concerned that it's not just the blood pressure, and it's not just the weight.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Does that mean when the doctor's getting this data from the kit, are they communicating at all with the patient and saying, “Hey you're looking, the numbers are good.” Or are they just saying, by exception, they'll communicate if the numbers don't look good?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Typically, I mean, the way we've set it up, is that we alert them if there's an issue. For example, blood pressure's too high. Could be symptomatic of something called preeclampsia. This is very dangerous, right? So we'll obviously communicate concerns in that area. But if things are okay, and there are no triggers, most providers — because they're very busy — most doctors don't want to be bothered with a lot of data.

turns.speaker: Juan Pablo
turns.text: The goal here, and as we continue to align the product, it's really focused on being able to show that remote monitoring can start to move the needle in outcomes. Right? And that's, for example, the fact that we've had two interventions through our program, where we've saved someone's, two pregnancies we detected preeclampsia, and we were able to triage that to the doctor. So…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That’s great.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But just so you know, that would have been, I mean a doctor's visit would have found that out as well.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Well, the problem is that there are gaps, right, in between the doctor's offices. So they're waiting sometimes two, three, four weeks in between appointments.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: We're capturing, on average, about 1.5 data points a week. So we're three times as likely, right, to detect a problem like that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Why can't the woman just have a cuff and step on the scale and put it into the app? I mean, and just communicate it with the doctor that way? This is my, have a little piece, a little calendar in the app, and every day she just goes in, tells what her weight is, tells what her blood pressure is once a week, and you're good to go.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: If I could just interject.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: On his behalf, I think the difference is, they're harmonizing the data and looking for irrelevant data points before the doctor even sees it. If the patient has to look at the data...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Well there's no data. You take your weight, you take your blood pressure, done.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Oh yeah. But that data is automatically sent to the cloud. What if there's a missed input, data point, where — what ends up happening is, if you’re not controlling the flow, and delivering, for example, devices that actually are accurate.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So there's all that process we're taking care of, and that’s what’s driving...

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: How many births are there in the U.S. a year?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So, four million births.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Okay, and about 60% are low risk?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah. 60% are low risk. Yep.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: What was the compliancy from your study?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: The compliance?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah, so we published, and it's actually a lot higher now, but we captured 75% of women every week were taking their weight, their blood pressure and using our app. Now, amongst our customer base, we're at around 90% compliant.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: But now we're in more than ten health systems around the country.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So what does that represent in terms of patients?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah so, right now we have a thousand patients under management.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So the doctors are your customers?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: In order for anything in digital healthcare to work, you have to work with the most trusted channel and partner in the healthcare experience. And that's the doctor. I could have gone consumer. And I think, sure, maybe I would have generated a million dollars, maybe, extra in sales. But really my goal is to build a billion-dollar company.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: The doctor is paying you for access to the data about their patients?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: For the entire experience. So essentially, we’ll go to them and say, “we have an incredible 21st-century experience that you can offer to your patients and so you should purchase from us, and we'll also help you make more money for every pregnancy that you deliver.”

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How do they make more money?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah so this is, it's very specific to how doctors get paid. Doctors in this country get paid something called a Global Fee for managing the entire pregnancy. So essentially, it's like a lump sum payment for managing the pre-natal care, the time spent delivering the child, then one post-partum visit. So it doesn't matter if a patient goes in 40 times or five times, the doctor gets paid the exact same amount of money.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So we essentially help the doctors make more money because we allow them to still make the same amount of money, but they see pregnant patients about 40% less often in the office. And so they have 40% more time that they can use on another procedure, seeing more patients. And typically, a practice will make about $600 more per pregnancy, and the cost of Babyscripts is $300. So they make about 100% return on investment when they work with us.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: And again, how do you mitigate the risk of a C-section? How are you able to intervene if a patient is gaining too much weight in between visits? Well you need a system that can capture incredible amounts of data in between appointments and essentially intervene behaviorally if there are issues. And Babyscripts, we've created the piping to be able to do that.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What do you make of the existential risk of the insurance companies changing their compensation plans and methods so that now they're not getting paid one lump sum for the whole pregnancy. And they're getting paid per appointment, that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: I don't see that happening. I see it actually going the other way, which is it's going to be more and more focused on finding more things to include in that lump sum so that they don't have to pay as much for more services or problems that occur in the pregnancy.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How much revenue have you generated to date?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: I mean, it's around $400,000.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: In the last...? Because you've launched over the last year.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah, so it's basically been, this year is like our first-year revenue.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So this is like the first year for us. And so, yeah, I mean, we've booked already $400,000. I believe I can get to around $700,000 by the end of this year with all of the deals we have in our pipeline. I mean, if you really think about what we're doing —

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: — and this is where I think it really gets interesting — the model we've delivered is actually triple aim healthcare. Because we're reducing the cost of care, we're improving access to care — so we reduce the cost of care by 40%, we improve access to care because you can get care wherever you are through the app and the devices — and we're actually improving outcomes. So that literally, we've had interventions where we've saved lives. Babyscripts has done that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So what are you raising? And what are the terms?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah, we're raising 3.5 million to really expand our sales reach and onboard 20 more customers, health system customers.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You're raising $3.5 million and the valuation is what?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Yeah. So it's a $10 million pre-money.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How much of the $3.5 million do you have committed so far?

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: So about $2.5 million.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Well, I really like what you're doing. Making great progress. I feel like you've attacked this problem in a smart way by starting with the studies to prove the efficacy, to prove what you're doing, because you know that that's what they're going to require, your customers are going to require. So I think you've approached it in a smart way. I'd like to participate.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: That's awesome.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So I'm in for $250,000.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Oh wow. Okay. That's awesome. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I, um, I love this. For so many reasons. I'm personally and professionally connected to this. So what I'd like to do is I'd like to do $500,000.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Oh geez. Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And what I'd like to do with that is — and just to be clear, I have a venture fund which is Structure Capital, and I have my own. So I would like to bring this to them to either do all of the $500,000, or to break this out so that I do a piece of this, they do a piece of this, and then our LPs, who get to directly invest, have the opportunity to do this. But I'd like you to carve out $500,000 for us.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Oh wow. Okay. Yeah, that's awesome. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You’re welcome

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I love you. I think you know this business amazingly well. Answered all the questions immaculately. I think you have the prescription for success.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Oh nice.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: That a good one? … I too really want to invest in this company. I think your round is all of a sudden over-subscribed. So I'm feeling a little like I've got to be scrappy here. We're a small fund. I'd like to do $50,000. But I think what you're working on is amazing. I think you're making a difference in the world, a positive difference. And I think you're going to make a boatload of money. And when I can combine those two things, it really gets me excited.

turns.speaker: Juan-Pablo
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So Howie, can we make it quadruplets?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Let's do it. I mean, look, it's a no-brainer to me. This exactly fits my thesis for my fund. I'm even smaller than Jake's, so I write $25 to $50 K checks. But I think those are the types of projects that I like to put myself into, that I like to participate in. Not only as an investor, but also as a partner, to sort of help, because that's what gets me up in the morning. So this directly fits the type of deal that I really get excited about, and I'd like to be in for $30,000.
